title: Longest Square Streak
description:
# Longest Square Streak

Given an array of positive integers `nums`, find the longest chain of distinct values where every next value is the square of the previous value.

A chain has the form:

`x, x^2, x^4, x^8, ...`

Every value in the chain must appear in `nums`. Duplicate copies of the same value do not increase the chain length; treat the input as a set of available values for this problem. The value `1` squares to itself, so it can only contribute one value and cannot form an infinite or duplicate-driven chain.

Return the maximum chain length. If no chain has length at least `2`, return `-1`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [4,3,6,16,8,2]
**Output:** 3

**Explanation:** The longest chain is `2 -> 4 -> 16`.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [2,3,5,6,7]
**Output:** -1

**Explanation:** No value has its square in the array.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10^5`
* `1 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`

tests.description: complete odd-base square chain up to the limit
a single value is not a valid streak
duplicates do not inflate the chain length
1 cannot form a chain with itself through duplicates
ignore self-looping ones and still find 4 -> 16
square near the upper value limit
choose the longer chain among multiple roots
unordered input with a longer non-two root

solutions.name: Hash Set Forward Walk
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert every distinct value into a hash set. For each distinct starting value, repeatedly square the current value while the next value is still present and still within the allowed numeric range.

## Key Insight

The sequence grows extremely quickly, so each walk has only a few steps before exceeding `10^9`. The special case `1` must stop immediately because `1 * 1 = 1`; otherwise duplicate `1` values could be mistaken for a longer chain.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log log V), where `V` is the largest value
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Sorted Root Dynamic Programming
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort the distinct values. For a value `x`, if it has an integer square root `r` that appeared earlier, the best chain ending at `x` is one more than the best chain ending at `r`. Otherwise it starts a new chain of length one.

## Key Insight

Sorting guarantees the square root is processed before its square. Skipping the self-root transition for `1` prevents `1` from extending itself through duplicate input values.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Chain Roots Only
solutions.description:
## Approach

A value should start a walk only if its integer square root is not also present. After finding those true roots, walk each root forward by repeated squaring and count the length.

## Key Insight

Starting only at roots avoids recounting the same chain from every internal value. For example, if `2`, `4`, and `16` are present, only `2` starts the chain; `4` is skipped because its square root is present.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n log log V)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Memoized Square DFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat each distinct value as a node with at most one outgoing edge to its square. Use memoized DFS to compute the longest chain starting from each value, caching the result so every value is solved once.

## Key Insight

The graph is almost a set of directed paths because every value points only to its square. The only self-loop is `1`, so the DFS handles `1` as a terminal length-one node before following square edges.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
